Threat.value: My body reacts to danger before I have even had time to think
I wake during the night to check whether I am safe
I scan for exits as soon as I enter any room or building

Memory.value: The memory feels like it is happening right now rather than something that is over
When I have memories of what happened I sometimes hear things in my head that I heard during the frightening event.
Something in my surroundings can instantly bring back the full memory without warning

Negative Appraisals.value: I have to be on guard all the time
If I think about the event, I will not be able to handle it
I have to be especially careful because you never know what can happen next

issues.item: Triggers: Being Praised: Receiving praise or positive attention
issues.explanation: 'Being praised' is a hard-to-explain trigger in a profile otherwise centered on a life-threatening accident with sensory trigger cues, intrusive reliving, and hypervigilant threat monitoring. Unlike smell or darkness, praise has no evident link to the accident-based memory/threat pattern and stands out as clinically incoherent unless additional interpersonal trauma context were present.

issues.item: Negative Appraisals: Institutional Failure: The people or institutions that should have protected me let me down
issues.explanation: 'Institutional failure' fits betrayal, assault, military, or disaster-response contexts more naturally than a single life-threatening accident in a financial analyst. In this profile the other appraisals focus on danger and inability to cope; this item introduces a qualitatively different blame/betrayal theme that is not supported by the trauma type, trigger pattern, or memory content.

vignette: John is a 63-year-old male of Oceania ethnicity who has been experiencing significant distress since a life-threatening accident that occurred several months ago. John's trauma began on a dark and stormy night when he was driving home from work. A sudden downpour made the roads extremely slippery, causing his car to skid off the road and crash into a tree. The smell of gasoline permeated the air as the vehicle quickly filled with smoke, leaving him trapped inside for several terrifying moments before emergency services arrived. Since that night, John has been plagued by vivid memories of the accident. The smell of burning rubber or gasoline can instantly trigger intense flashbacks, making it feel like he is reliving the experience all over again. This olfactory trigger often occurs in his daily routine, such as when passing a gas station on his commute to work. These moments make him freeze, his heart pounding with fear, before he even has time to consciously recognize what's happening. John's hypervigilance and scanning behaviors have become deeply ingrained. He constantly checks for exits whenever he enters any room or building, believing it is essential to ensure he can escape quickly if needed. At night, he often wakes up abruptly, his mind racing as he checks if the house is secure and safe from danger. This persistent vigilance has taken a toll on both his sleep and overall well-being. His work environment, as a Financial Analyst in a bustling office, has become another source of stress. The constant sound of cars driving by during his morning commute or the occasional engine noise from nearby construction can trigger intense anxiety, making it difficult for him to focus at work. John's colleagues have noticed that he often seems distracted and on edge. John's marriage has also been affected by these changes. His wife, Alice, finds herself having to reassure him multiple times a day that everything is okay. John has come to believe that if he allows himself to think about the event, he will not be able to handle it, leading to increased avoidance of any reminders or discussions related to the accident. This has created tension in their relationship, as Alice feels helpless and frustrated by his reluctance to share his feelings. Despite these difficulties, John's fear of losing control remains a powerful deterrent from seeking help. He is certain that if he allows himself to confront his fears, it will be too much for him to bear. However, the relentless nature of his symptoms has started to interfere with his daily functioning and personal relationships more than ever before. What finally brought John to seek help was an episode where he became extremely anxious while at a movie theater, triggered by the smell of popcorn mixed with the darkness and ambient sounds of traffic from outside. He felt overwhelmed and believed that he had no choice but to get professional assistance. In therapy, John hopes to regain control over his life and find ways to manage his symptoms without resorting to avoidance or constant vigilance. John's journey so far has been marked by a profound sense of vulnerability and fear. His negative appraisals have made it difficult for him to trust that he can navigate the world without constant threat monitoring. Yet, beneath these fears lies a desire to reconnect with his life and relationships in a meaningful way, free from the paralyzing grip of his traumatic memories.
